title: The lens: 24 mm to 2000 mm
teaches: What focal length really changes, why a far moon looks huge behind a near tree, when cropping beats zooming, and the air between you and the subject

blocks.text: **The challenge.** You have seen the picture: a full moon rising enormous behind a single tree on a ridge, the tree a dark cut-out against the bright disc. You try it from the road below the ridge with the lens at 200 mm, and get the left-hand picture: a nice pine and a small white moon floating above it. Zooming in only makes the pine bigger. The right-hand picture is the same pine and the same moon, and nothing has been pasted in. The difference is that the photographer was standing about seven kilometres away.[^moon-sunset]

blocks.caption: A pine on a ridge and the rising moon, at 200 mm and at 2000 mm

blocks.text: A second puzzle from the same evening: a heron on the far side of a marina, too far to fill the frame even at 2000 mm. Should you zoom all the way and hope, or take it at 1000 mm and crop later? Both questions come down to what a lens's focal length does and, more to the point, what it does not do.

The [[focal length|aperture]] decides how wide a slice of the world lands on the sensor. A short focal length takes in a wide wedge; a long one, a narrow wedge, which is then spread across the same sensor, so everything in it looks bigger. The P950's lens really runs from 4.3 mm to 357 mm, but its sensor is so small that those numbers would mean little to anyone used to other cameras. So Nikon quotes the **equivalent** focal lengths, 24 mm to 2000 mm: the focal lengths that would give the same wedge on a standard 36 × 24 mm frame, 5.6 times the real ones.

blocks.caption: The wedge of the world the P950 takes in, from 24 mm to 2000 mm
blocks.task: Zoom past 800 mm and watch the wedge close

blocks.text: At 24 mm the frame takes in about 74 degrees side to side, a whole hillside. At 2000 mm it takes in about one degree, the width of your little finger held at arm's length.[^finger] Zooming does not bring you any closer. It throws away everything outside a narrower wedge and enlarges what is left.

Photographers say a long lens "compresses" a scene, stacking a far hill right up against a near bird. It is a useful word for a real effect, but the lens is not doing it. How big two things look against each other depends only on how far away each one is. The moon is 384,000 kilometres away, so walking a few kilometres changes its size not at all; the pine is near, so every step back makes it smaller. Back away far enough and the pine shrinks until the moon is bigger than it. The long lens is what lets you then fill the frame with that pair.

blocks.caption: A pine 18 m tall on a ridge, and the full moon rising behind it
blocks.task: Make the moon fill at least half the frame's height behind the pine

blocks.text: Try **Stay put** and zoom: the moon and the pine grow together and their sizes keep the same ratio, because neither got farther away. Then **Walk back**: the camera retreats as the lens lengthens, so the pine stays the same size in the frame, and the moon swells behind it. At 2000 mm, to keep an 18 m pine a fifth of the frame's height, you have to stand about seven kilometres away.

This is a picture you plan rather than stumble on. You need a spot about seven kilometres from the tree, in line with where the moon will rise, and the moon has to come up exactly behind it, which a planning app or a map and a compass can tell you. Arrive early, frame the tree, and wait, but not long: the moon moves its own width in about two minutes, so at 2000 mm the moment behind the tree is short.[^moon-exposure] The same rule works on a smaller scale with a bird: step back and zoom in, and the hills behind it grow and close in.

The heron across the marina is a question about pixels. The P950's sensor is 4608 pixels across. At 2000 mm, suppose the heron fills a quarter of that width, and you would like it a quarter of the finished picture. Taken at 1000 mm, it fills an eighth, so you have to crop the picture to half its width, and the crop keeps 2304 pixels across instead of 4608. Cropping is the same as zooming, except that it costs pixels.

blocks.caption: The heron kept at a quarter of the finished picture's width, at each zoom
blocks.task: Find a zoom of 1000 mm or less whose crop still fills a computer screen

blocks.text: So zoom first and crop second: every halving of the zoom halves the pixels you keep across, and quarters their total. But how many you need depends on how the picture will be seen. A phone screen is at most about 1080 pixels across, a computer screen 1920, and a sharp A4 print wants about 3500. A picture for a screen can survive a fair crop, and sometimes cropping is the better choice: a wider frame is easier to keep a moving bird in, and the lens is a little brighter at 1000 mm than at 2000 mm, with less air shimmer in the way (see below). The P950's digital zoom, which goes past 2000 mm, is a crop done inside the camera; you lose nothing by cropping yourself afterwards instead.

parts.title: Air is part of the lens

blocks.text: At 2000 mm you are looking through a long column of air, and on a warm day that air shimmers. Ground heated by the sun warms the air just above it, and pockets of warm and cool air bend light by slightly different amounts, so the picture wobbles and softens like the view over a hot road. At long range this, not the lens, is often what keeps a picture from being sharp, and no setting fixes it.

What helps is less air and calmer air. Get closer, so the column is shorter. Shoot early in the morning, before the ground warms, or on overcast days. Avoid shooting across sunlit tarmac, rooftops or dry fields; across cool water or grass is better. Haze, the bluish veil over distant hills, is a different thing, made of tiny particles, but it has the same cure: less air between you and what you are photographing. The moon shot works partly because almost all its distance is above the atmosphere.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Focal length sets how wide a wedge of the world reaches the sensor; equivalent focal lengths are 5.6 times the P950's real ones.
How big a far thing looks against a near one depends only on where you stand; the lens just frames the pair.
Stepping back and zooming in keeps the subject the same size and makes the background bigger.
Cropping is zooming that costs pixels: half the zoom keeps half the pixels across, a quarter of the total.
At long range, shimmering air often limits sharpness more than the lens does.

items.question: You photograph a heron with distant hills behind it at 200 mm, then zoom to 1000 mm without moving. How do the hills compare with the heron?
options: Their size relative to the heron is unchanged
They look bigger compared with the heron
They look smaller compared with the heron
They disappear from the frame entirely
items.why: Without moving, every distance stays the same, so both grow by the same factor. To make the hills bigger next to the heron, you would have to step back and zoom in.

items.question: Why does the P950 call its lens 24 to 2000 mm when it is really 4.3 to 357 mm?
options: They give the same view as on a 36 × 24 mm frame
The lens has a hidden extension inside the body
Nikon measures the lens from the back of the sensor
The numbers already include the digital zoom
items.why: On the small sensor, 357 mm takes in the same wedge as 2000 mm would on a full-frame camera. Equivalent numbers let people compare views across cameras.

items.question: A heron fills a quarter of the frame's width at 2000 mm. You shoot it at 500 mm and crop to the same framing. Roughly how many pixels across does the crop keep?
options: About 1150
About 2300
About 3500
All 4608
items.why: At 500 mm the heron is a quarter as wide, so the crop keeps a quarter of the width: 4608 ÷ 4, about 1150 pixels, enough for a phone but not a print.

items.question: On a hot afternoon, your 2000 mm shots of a deer 300 m away across a field are soft whatever you do. What is the most likely cause?
options: Heat shimmer in the air between you
The aperture is too wide for the scene
The ISO is too low for the light
The stabiliser is switched on
items.why: Warm air rising off the sunlit field bends light unevenly. Getting closer, or coming back in the cool of the morning, is the fix.

items.question: For a huge moon behind a lone tree on a ridge, what matters most?
options: Standing far from the tree and zooming in
Using the widest aperture the lens has
Getting as close to the tree as you can
Setting the camera's digital zoom to maximum
items.why: The moon's size cannot change, so the tree has to shrink, which means distance. The long lens then fills the frame with the pair.

items.question: When might a crop from 1000 mm be a better choice than a frame at 2000 mm?
options: For a fast bird in a picture meant for a screen
When making a large print of a perched bird
When the bird is already filling the frame
Never, since zooming is always better
items.why: A wider frame makes a fast bird easier to follow, and the lens is brighter at 1000 mm. A screen needs only about 1920 pixels across, which a moderate crop still leaves.

summary: **Focal length is a wedge.** It sets how wide a slice of the world reaches the sensor; zooming throws away the rest and enlarges what is left.
**Equivalent millimetres compare views.** The P950's real 4.3 to 357 mm give the views of 24 to 2000 mm on a full-frame camera.
**Compression is where you stand.** How big a far thing looks next to a near one depends only on their distances from you.
**Step back and zoom in for a big background.** The subject stays the same size and the background grows; a huge moon needs kilometres.
**Cropping is zooming that costs pixels.** Half the zoom keeps half the pixels across; a screen needs about 1920 across, a print about 3500.
**The air is part of the lens.** Heat shimmer softens long shots; get closer, and shoot in the cool of the morning.

moon-sunset.title: Why the full moon rises at sunset
moon-sunset.text: A full moon is the moon on the far side of the Earth from the sun, which is why its whole face is lit. Being opposite the sun, it rises as the sun sets, so the moonrise shot is a dusk shot: the sky still has some light in it, and the moon is low enough to sit behind a tree. A day or so before full, it rises a little before sunset, while the sky is brighter still, which many photographers prefer.

finger.title: Angles at arm's length
finger.text: Held at arm's length, a little finger is about one degree wide, a thumb about two, and a fist about ten. The moon is half a degree across, half a little finger, which is why it always looks smaller in photos than you remember: the eye judges it against the landscape, and a wide lens records it as the small thing it is.

moon-exposure.title: Exposing the moon
moon-exposure.text: The moon's face is lit by full sunlight, so it needs about the same exposure as a sunny landscape: roughly f/8 at 1/250 s and ISO 100. The dusk landscape around it needs several stops more, which is why the moonrise shot works best in the few minutes when the sky is still bright enough to hold the tree's outline. Later, either the moon is a white blob or the land is black.
